When edge 0 is conv3x3, node 2 still gets learned features via node 1 and edge 2, so deleting the direct 0->2 edge loses less.
With edge 4 removed, node 3 has fewer inputs, so a processed direct route from the input contributes more to the output sum.

With edge 0 pooled, a skip on edge 4 injects blurred, unprocessed features straight into the output sum, diluting it.

I kept 14 of the 20 hypotheses and replaced 6. The six I dropped either argued both directions equally well, or ran against a known benchmark fact.

**Dropped:**
- **#1 (e5 conv3x3 | e2 conv3x3, lower):** The best NAS-Bench-201 cells put conv3x3 on both edges, so they work together rather than saturating. The claimed direction is doubtful.
- **#9 (e5 conv1x1 | e2 none, lower):** The "why" makes the opposite case just as well.
- **#11 (e0 avg_pool | e4 conv3x3, higher):** The mechanism is speculative, and the stated risk of losing resolution twice could flip the sign.
- **#15 (e5 avg_pool | e1 conv3x3, higher):** Saying pooling "smooths rich features" is weak; pooling mostly hurts no matter what comes before it.
- **#16 (e1 conv3x3 | e2 conv1x1, lower):** The margin is likely small and not consistent across datasets.
- **#18 (e0 conv3x3 | e1 avg_pool, higher):** This is a weak indirect bottleneck argument. A same-edge condition captures the idea more cleanly.

**Replacements:** Five of the six use structural interactions, where an upstream `none` cuts a node off or a downstream `none` leaves a node with nowhere to go. Changes on edges in a dead or orphaned part of the graph can't affect accuracy, so these interactions should be large and the same on every dataset. The sixth uses a same-edge condition: switching an edge from `none` to conv3x3 also brings back the paths through it, so the gain should be bigger than switching from any other op.

**Kept** (plausible and non-trivial): #2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 12, 13, 14, 17, 19, 20. The residual and shortcut ideas (#3, 4, 13) agree with the skip_connect on edge 3 in the top-ranked cells.
